justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward bias in gold prices across all three horizons, starting from what I assumed was a base price in the neighborhood of $1,800–$1,815 per ounce at the time of the forecast. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to the prevailing spot price and applied a slight positive drift, reflecting gold's tendency to hold value or inch higher during periods of macro uncertainty. For the one-week estimate, I extended that drift modestly, accounting for the possibility that any short-term catalysts — such as Federal Reserve commentary, dollar movements, or geopolitical developments — would on balance support gold rather than weigh on it. For the one-month estimate, the upward drift grows a bit more, reflecting gold's longer-run tendency to appreciate when real interest rates are low or falling and when global uncertainty is elevated, both of which were plausible assumptions in the broader macro environment.

The width of the confidence intervals expands substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is a standard feature of forecasting any financial asset with mean-reverting and momentum-driven dynamics. At one day, gold prices are relatively sticky — the overnight range is typically contained unless there is a major scheduled event or shock — so my 90% interval spans roughly $130. At one week, I widened the band to $270 to capture the possibility of scheduled data releases (CPI, jobs reports, Fed speakers) shifting rate expectations meaningfully. At one month, the $560 range reflects the genuine difficulty of predicting gold over four-plus weeks, given how sensitive it is to shifts in the dollar index, Treasury yields, and broader risk sentiment.

The most meaningful risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals are on both tails. On the upside, a sudden escalation in geopolitical conflict, a sharp deterioration in U.S. economic data triggering aggressive Fed pivot expectations, or a significant dollar sell-off could drive gold well above $2,140 over the month. On the downside, a surprisingly hawkish Fed — whether through rate hikes or sustained restrictive rhetoric — paired with a strong dollar and rising real yields could crush gold below $1,580. Central bank policy surprises are particularly dangerous to these estimates because they can move gold by several percent in a single session, easily blowing through interval bounds that assume a relatively stable macro backdrop.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that my intervals, while wide at the monthly horizon, are still parametric in nature and may understate true tail risk. Gold has historically experienced sharp, discontinuous moves during crises — flash crashes, safe-haven demand spikes, or liquidity-driven selloffs — that fall outside what normal distributional assumptions capture.
